passage: Tejas, you're scared of Bruno next door? Let me tell you about your Vinita Nani at your age. In our town, the milkman's boy got bitten by a street dog, and the whole lane talked about it for a week: the blood, the injections, the crying. After that I decided every dog in the world wanted to bite me. I crossed the road for puppies. I screamed at our neighbour's old dog, who could barely stand. Once my father asked, "How many dogs have bitten anyone you know?" I said, "Lots!" He made me count. It was one. One boy, one dog. But that one story was so loud in my head, it felt like hundreds.

qa.q: What happened to the milkman's boy?
qa.a: The milkman's boy got bitten by a street dog.

qa.q: Why did young Vinita feel every dog wanted to bite her?
qa.a: Young Vinita felt afraid because the bite story was retold for a week with vivid details, so it filled her mind and felt like something that happened all the time, even though it was one case.

qa.q: What did Vinita's father do that helped, and how could Tejas try it?
qa.a: He asked her to count real bites among people she knew, which showed there was only one. Tejas could count the gentle dogs seen on the street against any that actually bit someone.

qa.q: How might the owner of the neighbour's old dog have felt when young Vinita screamed?
qa.a: The owner may have felt puzzled or hurt, since their old dog could barely stand and had done nothing to frighten anyone.

grounding: Shows a child who, after one vivid dog-bite story, decides all dogs are dangerous because the memorable case feels common.

passage: The school van broke down, so Disha and her brother Anand had to walk the last kilometre home in the drizzle. At the corner by the tea stall, three street dogs lay curled under a cart. Disha froze. Two days earlier, a classmate had told everyone about a cousin bitten on the leg who needed a big injection. "They'll bite us," she whispered. "All dogs bite." Anand pointed. "Those three have slept there all year. You pass them every day in the van." "That's different," she said, gripping his sleeve. The rain got heavier. She made them walk the long way round, past the temple, adding ten wet minutes, and glared at every dog she saw.

qa.q: Why did Disha and Anand have to walk the last kilometre?
qa.a: The school van broke down, so they had to walk the last kilometre home in the drizzle.

qa.q: Why does Disha feel sure that all dogs bite?
qa.a: Disha feels frightened because the classmate's story of the bitten cousin and the big injection is fresh and scary. That fear feels more real than the many days the same dogs slept quietly by the cart.

qa.q: What small step could help Disha the next time they pass those dogs?
qa.a: Anand could help her count how many times she has passed them without trouble, and they could walk by calmly together, giving the dogs plenty of space.

qa.q: What is it like for Anand when Disha insists on the long way?
qa.a: Anand has to walk ten extra minutes in heavy rain, and may feel both annoyed and protective, since his calm facts can't beat her scary story.

grounding: Shows a girl who heard one vivid bite story deciding all dogs bite, even the ones she passes safely every day.

passage: Ever since the residents' group shared a clip of a boy being chased by a dog in another city, ten-year-old Zainab had refused to go down to the play area of their Tolichowki apartment block. "Moti will bite me," she said, though Moti, the watchman's brown dog, usually just slept by the gate and let the toddlers pull his ears. Rehana, her mother, sat with her on the balcony. "How many children here has Moti bitten?" Zainab thought. "None... but he could." "And how many times have you watched that clip?" "Eleven," Zainab admitted. "Everyone keeps sending it." Down below, her friends shrieked with laughter on the swings.

qa.q: How many times had Zainab watched the clip?
qa.a: Zainab admitted she had watched the clip eleven times.

qa.q: Why does Moti seem dangerous to Zainab even though he has bitten no one?
qa.a: Zainab is scared because the clip, sent again and again, fills her mind and makes a bite feel likely, even though Moti only sleeps and lets toddlers pull his ears.

qa.q: How could Rehana help Zainab get back to the play area?
qa.a: Rehana could go down with her, watch Moti together from a distance and notice how he actually behaves, while skipping new forwards of the clip for a while.

qa.q: How might Zainab's friends on the swings see her staying upstairs?
qa.a: They may miss her and not understand why, since to them Moti is just the sleepy dog by the gate.

grounding: Shows a girl who keeps seeing one scary dog clip deciding the gentle colony dog is dangerous.

passage:
"Zainab, come see! Pepper learned to sit!"
"No, Aditi baji. I'm staying on the sofa."
"She's a puppy. She's this big."
"Rehan in my class said a dog bit his neighbour's leg and he needed injections. Dogs bite."
Aditi's mother came in with a plate of pakoras. "Zainab, how many dogs do you know?"
Zainab thought. "Pepper. Nanu's dog. The shop dog. The white one at school."
"Have any of them bitten anyone?"
"...No. But Rehan's story."
"One story is very loud, isn't it?" said Aditi's mother. "It shouts over all the quiet ones."
Pepper wobbled over and sniffed Zainab's sock. Zainab pulled her feet up fast. Then, very slowly, she put one finger down. Pepper licked it.
"Eww," said Zainab. But she didn't pull back.

qa.q: What trick had Pepper learned?
qa.a: Pepper learned to sit.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Zainab that dogs bite?
qa.a: Rehan's bite story made Zainab scared, and because it was so easy to remember it seemed like what dogs usually do. The many dogs she knows that never bit anyone didn't come to mind.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make at the end, and why was it a good small step?
qa.a: She slowly put one finger down for Pepper. Testing the fear a little at a time let a real, gentle dog start to outweigh the scary story.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when Zainab refuses to meet Pepper?
qa.a: Aditi is probably disappointed, since she was excited to show off the new puppy, and may want her cousin to see how gentle Pepper is.

grounding: A young girl hears one scary dog-bite story and decides all dogs bite, even a small puppy at her cousin's home.

passage: I'm Vaibhav, and as a boy of nine I feared every dog in the world. It started when my cousin Indu told me about a boy at her school who got bitten by a stray. She did the growl and the scream. After that, I saw that bite whenever I saw a dog. I crossed the road when I saw Bholu, our neighbour's old dog, though he just sleeps by the gate and had licked my hand a hundred times. I told Ma, "All dogs bite, it's true, Indu said." Ma asked, "How many dogs have bitten you?" None. I still didn't pat Bholu for a long time. Now I do. He's very soft. And Indu admits she made the growl louder than it was.

qa.q: What was the name of the neighbour's old dog?
qa.a: Bholu.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav cross the road even to avoid Bholu?
qa.a: Indu's dramatic story with the growl and the scream was so vivid that it came to mind every time he saw any dog. It felt more real than all the times Bholu had licked his hand.

qa.q: What question from Ma could help Vaibhav, and how might he use it next time?
qa.a: "How many dogs have bitten you?" Next time a scary story makes him afraid, he can count what has really happened to him before deciding something is always true.

qa.q: How might Indu feel knowing her story scared Vaibhav for so long?
qa.a: She might feel a bit guilty, which is why she now admits she made the growl louder than it was.

grounding: A boy recalls how one vivid bite story from his cousin made him fear every dog, even a gentle old neighbour's dog.
